Worldly describes someone or something that belongs to, or is shaped by, the real, everyday world of human experience — especially its practical, social, and material side.

The word carries two closely related main senses. Understanding both will give you a complete picture.
Sense 1: Experienced, Sophisticated, and Wise About Life

When you call a person worldly, you mean they have broad experience of life. They have seen how the world actually works — not how it ideally should work, but how it really does. They understand people: their motivations, their flaws, their games. They are not easily shocked, fooled, or misled.

A worldly person has typically been exposed to different cultures, different social classes, different kinds of people, and the harder realities of life. Because of this exposure, they develop a kind of practical wisdom and social sophistication. They know how to read a room. They understand unspoken rules. They can navigate complex or morally grey situations without falling apart.

Think of it this way: imagine two people walking into a difficult negotiation, or a new city, or a complicated social situation. One is wide-eyed, trusting, and unprepared for the tricks and realities of the world. The other has been around, has dealt with all kinds of people, and knows exactly what to expect. The second person is worldly.

Example sentences:

  • "She was a worldly woman — she had lived in five countries, worked in business, and could spot dishonesty from a mile away."
  • "For a nineteen-year-old, he had surprisingly worldly views about money and power."
  • "Her worldly experience made her the perfect person to negotiate the deal."
Sense 2: Relating to the Material World, Not the Spiritual One

The second sense is used especially in religious, philosophical, or moral contexts. Here, "worldly" means belonging to this physical, earthly life — as opposed to spiritual, divine, or eternal matters.

In this sense, "worldly things" means money, possessions, status, physical pleasure, ambition, fame — the stuff of ordinary earthly life. When someone contrasts "worldly concerns" with "spiritual concerns," they mean the difference between chasing success and wealth in this life versus focusing on the soul, God, or inner peace.

This use comes from the idea that "the world" (in a spiritual sense) refers to the realm of human desires, material comfort, and earthly attachments. A saint or a deeply religious person might be called unworldly — meaning they have let go of material desires.

Example sentences:

  • "The monk gave up all his worldly possessions — his house, his car, his savings — and entered the monastery."
  • "She found that worldly success — the promotions, the money, the status — left her feeling empty."
  • "The priest warned his congregation not to be too attached to worldly pleasures."
  • "He had achieved every worldly goal he had set for himself, yet something was missing."
The Two Senses Side by Side

Both senses share the same underlying idea: "worldly" always refers to this world — the real, physical, human world — rather than something innocent, sheltered, naive, ideal, or spiritual. When applied to a person, it means they are shaped by and wise to that world. When applied to things (possessions, pleasures, success), it means those things belong to earthly life.
What Worldly Is Not — The Key Contrasts

Understanding a word's opposites sharpens your understanding enormously.

Worldly ↔ Naïve / Innocent
A naïve person believes the best about everything and everyone. They haven't yet learned about the world's complexities, deceptions, and harsh realities. A worldly person has moved past that innocence — not bitterly, but practically.

Worldly ↔ Sheltered
A sheltered person has been protected from difficult experiences. They may be kind and intelligent, but they haven't been tested by the world. A worldly person has been out there — exposed, challenged, and shaped by experience.

Worldly ↔ Idealistic
An idealistic person believes the world should be — and can be — fair, perfect, and good. A worldly person doesn't reject goodness, but they don't expect perfection either. They are realistic about human nature.

Worldly ↔ Spiritual / Otherworldly
In the second sense, the direct opposite is someone who has renounced or risen above material desires — a monk, an ascetic, or simply a deeply spiritual person focused on inner life rather than external success.
Positive or Negative? It Depends on Context

This is an important nuance. "Worldly" is not always purely positive or purely negative — it depends on who is speaking and what they value.

When it's a compliment: In everyday secular conversation, calling someone worldly is usually admiring. You're saying they are sophisticated, experienced, and capable. They won't be easily cheated. They understand how things work. This is someone you'd trust in a tough situation.

When it's a criticism: In religious or deeply moral contexts, calling someone "too worldly" is a gentle criticism. It means they are overly focused on material things — money, status, pleasure — and not enough on deeper values or spiritual life. A religious teacher might warn: "Don't be so worldly that you forget what truly matters."

So the word itself is neutral; the tone comes from context.

Someone can be more or less worldly. A young person who has traveled, worked, and dealt with difficult situations might be described as surprisingly worldly for their age. Someone who has never left their hometown, always been protected, and trusts everyone might be not very worldly at all — which could be said warmly (they have an innocence about them) or as a gentle warning (they might be taken advantage of).

• Worldliness (noun): the quality of being worldly. "Her worldliness showed in the way she handled every difficult person with ease."
  • Worldly-wise (adjective): means exactly the same as worldly in Sense 1, but slightly more emphatic — wise specifically in the ways of the world. "He was worldly-wise enough to know that not every promise would be kept."
  • Unworldly (adjective): the direct opposite — innocent, naive, or spiritually focused rather than practically experienced. "She was brilliant but somewhat unworldly — she had spent her whole life in academic research."
A Summary to Anchor It All

Worldly = shaped by, wise to, or belonging to the real, material, human world.

  • About a person: experienced, sophisticated, not naïve, understands how life and people really work.
  • About things: belonging to earthly, material life (possessions, success, pleasure) rather than spiritual or ideal concerns.

If you meet someone who has lived fully — who has navigated the world's complexities with open eyes and come out wiser for it — you might say: "She's worldly." That says everything.
